title: Labels, legends and subplots
summary: Make a chart readable without you in the room, and put several charts on one figure.

steps.title: A chart must explain itself
body: A chart is read without you there to explain it. Every chart needs:
- a **title** that says what it shows (better: what it *means*: "Sales doubled after the March campaign"),
- a **legend** when there are several series,
ax.set(title="...", xlabel="...", ylabel="...")    # all at once

steps.title: Label it properly
prompt: The chart in the editor works but explains nothing. Fix `plot_revenue(months, revenue)` so the chart has the
title `Monthly revenue, 2024`, x label `Month`, y label `Revenue (EUR)`, and x tick labels rotated 45 degrees
steps.starter:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def plot_revenue(months, revenue):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    ax.plot(months, revenue, marker="o")
    return fig, ax

steps.title: Subplots: a grid of axes
body: `plt.subplots(rows, cols)` makes a figure with a grid of axes and returns them as a NumPy array:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))   # one row, two columns
fig.suptitle("Sales overview")                    # a title for the whole figure
Use `sharey=True` when the panels must be compared on the same scale; otherwise each panel picks its own range,
and a small bar on one can look as tall as a big bar on another.

steps.explain: A 2 x 3 grid holds six axes. `fig.axes` lists them row by row, so index 5 is the bottom-right panel.

steps.prompt: Two panels compare monthly sales of two shops; one sells ten times more than the other. Why pass `sharey=True`?
options: So the same height means the same value on both panels
So both panels share one legend
It is required when there are two panels
So the bars are drawn in the same colour
steps.explain: Without it, each panel scales to its own data, and the small shop looks as busy as the big one.

steps.prompt: Arrange the code to build a two-panel figure: create the grid, then draw and title the left panel, then the right panel, and add the figure title last.
steps.explain: Create the grid first; then each panel's drawing and title can come in any sensible order.

steps.title: A two-panel overview
prompt: Write `overview(months, revenue, totals)` that returns `(fig, axes)` for a figure with **one row of two axes**:
- left: a line of `revenue` over `months`, titled `Revenue`,
- right: a bar chart of the dict `totals` (`{region: value}`), titled `By region`,
steps.starter:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def overview(months, revenue, totals):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
    return fig, ax
hints: `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2)`; `axes[0]` is the left panel.
template: Dojo.eq("left is a line titled Revenue", (1, "Revenue"), (len(dojo_l.get_lines()), dojo_l.get_title()) if dojo_l else None)
Dojo.eq("right is two bars titled By region", (2, "By region"), (len(dojo_r.patches), dojo_r.get_title()) if dojo_r else None)
Dojo.check("side by side, not stacked", dojo_l is not None and dojo_r is not None and dojo_l.get_position().x0 < dojo_r.get_position().x0, "use plt.subplots(1, 2)")

steps.title: Small multiples
prompt: Write `small_multiples(df)` where `df` has columns `month`, `region` and `sales`. Make **one panel per region**
in a single row (regions in sorted order), all sharing the y axis (`sharey=True`). Each panel shows that region's
`sales` over `month` as a line and is titled with the region name. Return `(fig, axes)`.
Filter rows with a boolean mask: `df[df["region"] == region]`.
steps.starter:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def small_multiples(df):

for ax, region in zip(axes, regions):
